stories.title: Now Is the Time to Buy in Commercial Real Estate: Morgan Stanley
stories.excerpt: Despite a bumpy economy and increasingly high Treasury yields, one global investment firm believes now is the time to pounce on U.S. commercial real estate. Commercial Observer spoke with Tony Charles, global head of research and strategy at Morgan Stanley Real Estate Investing, who outlined the main takeaways from Morgan Stanley Investment Management’s mid-year 2026 real estate outlook. After a four-year recession, commercial real estate is now being repriced, giving investors a chance to acquire prime assets at low prices; supply is down across the board; and megatrends in AI, global supply chains, and aging demographics have opened up attractive entry points into infrastructure, retail and senior housing. “We certainly believe we’re entering the next up-cycle for real estate. It’s an attractive entry point,” Charles told CO in a Thursday interview. “And, given the repricing that’s now below replacement costs, we’re pretty confident in the next vintage of real estate investing.” Charles argued that the recent U.S. real estate downturn — which began in mid-2022 amid the Federal Reserve’s policy U-turn to hike interest rates coming out of COVID-19 — created “the longest downturn for real estate since the 1980s and early 1990s,” and that four years later, pricing is still down an average of 20 percent across the board. But he noted that “supply is down dramatically, so that’s obviously very helpful for real estate,” and that a strong structural macroeconomic backdrop — U.S. GDP grew 2.1 percent year-over-year in the second quarter of 2026 — has provided “a lot of green shoots that are beginning to show through.” He pointed out that CRE transaction activity increased 23 percent year-over-year in the U.S., institutional capital raising is up nearly 40 percent on the year, and that CRE debt originations are up around 20 percent year-over-year. bullets: Morgan Stanley: U.S. CRE entering next up-cycle after four-year recession, pricing now below replacement cost.
Supply down across board; megatrends in AI, supply chains, aging demographics opening entry points.
Repricing creates attractive acquisition window for institutional investors across multiple asset classes.
stories.summary: Morgan Stanley Investment Management's mid-year 2026 outlook signals inflection: after a four-year CRE downturn that began mid-2022, assets are now repriced below replacement costs with constrained supply across sectors. The firm identifies AI, global supply-chain reshoring, and demographic aging as structural tailwinds supporting the next investment vintage. Charles positioned current conditions as an optimal entry point for prime assets given renewed capital availability.
stories.impact: Signals broader capital market thaw and investor appetite recovery across geographies and asset types. For multifamily developers, this means easier financing terms, lower equity hurdle rates, and validation to underwrite new starts in core markets—particularly in metros benefiting from AI job clusters, supply-chain nearshoring (Texas, Southeast), and senior housing demand (Sun Belt, high cost-of-living metros). Expect cap rates to remain compressed and more institutional equity chasing deals through 2026.

stories.title: Lincoln, ACORE Converting Historic SLC Foundry
stories.excerpt: Lincoln Property Company and ACORE CAPITAL launched Foundry43, the new identity for the former Industry SLC historic structure. The property was created through the adaptive reuse of a distinctive industrial landmark in Salt Lake City. (photo courtesy Salt Lake Tribune) ACORE enlisted Lincoln to help stabilize and reposition this mixed-use development at the former steel foundry site. Together, the partners have been making meaningful investments into the property to restart construction and have now completed the parking structure and retail space. The Former Industry SLC building Reimagined as Foundry43 will build upon the existing 230,000 square foot office campus by delivering 64,000 square feet of additional creative office space, a 34,000 square foot fitness center, 12,000 square feet of new retail, and a 1,000-stall parking garage in the heart of the Granary Neighborhood. JLL has been retained to lead leasing efforts for the property. The post Lincoln, ACORE Converting Historic SLC Foundry appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Lincoln Property / ACORE: reposition historic SLC foundry into Foundry43 mixed-use campus with 230k SF office base.
Phase II adds 64k SF creative office, 34k SF fitness center, 12k SF retail, 1,000-stall parking garage.
Adaptive reuse in Granary neighborhood; JLL leading leasing for office and creative space.
stories.summary: Lincoln Property Company and ACORE Capital completed parking and retail phases of Foundry43, a major adaptive reuse of an industrial landmark in Salt Lake City's Granary neighborhood. The repositioned 230,000-square-foot office campus will expand by 64,000 SF of creative office, a 34,000-SF fitness center, 12,000 SF of retail, and a 1,000-stall parking structure. JLL is managing leasing efforts.
stories.impact: Minimal direct impact on multifamily. However, signals market validation for Salt Lake City's urban infill: office-led mixed-use redevelopment and amenity density (fitness, parking, retail) in historic neighborhoods suggest landlord confidence in downtown worker/resident attraction. Indirectly supports multifamily case for building near creative office clusters and transit-oriented adaptive reuse zones in SLC's core—i.e., if Class A creative office thrives at Granary, nearby residential will follow.

stories.title: RangeWater Spends $55M on Atlanta Rental Community
stories.excerpt: Bell Partners sold Bell Buckhead West for $54.9 million. RangeWater Residential was the buyer. Bell Partners paid $62 million to acquire the asset in 2017, which is at 3201 Downwood Cir. in Atlanta. RangeWater renamed the property Blaine Buckhead West. Rents at Blaine Buckhead West range from $1,399 to $2,345. Unit sizes range from 676 square feet for a studio to 1,189 square feet for a two-bedroom unit. The 280-unit project was built in 2015. Amenities include a fitness center, pool, 24-hour Java Bar and Lounge, Bocce Ball Court, game room with pool table, and a Sky Lounge Rooftop Deck. Sun Life Financial announced acquired Bell Partners for $350 million. As part of the arrangement, Bell Partners became part of Sun Life’s multifamily operating platform. The post RangeWater Spends $55M on Atlanta Rental Community appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: RangeWater acquired 280-unit Bell Buckhead West for $54.9M; Bell Partners paid $62M in 2017 (8-year loss).
Rents $1,399–$2,345; 2015-built; Sun Life Financial recently acquired Bell Partners for $350M platform.
Market signal: distressed-asset trading in Atlanta Buckhead; below-replacement acquisitions driving mark-to-market resets.
stories.summary: RangeWater Residential purchased the 280-unit Bell Buckhead West in Atlanta for $54.9 million, down from the $62 million Bell Partners paid in 2017—an 11% loss over eight years. The 2015-built community offers studios to two-bedrooms at rents ranging $1,399–$2,345. The sale follows Sun Life Financial's $350 million acquisition of Bell Partners, integrating it into Sun Life's multifamily operating platform.
stories.impact: Reinforces Atlanta's repricing cycle: investors marking down older, non-premium Class B assets (pre-2016 vintage, standard amenities) as Class A supply absorbs quality renters and rate-growth stalls. RangeWater's acquisition suggests value-add play via amenity refresh and operational tightening. For developers in Atlanta metro, this signals cap-rate floor compression—new construction must justify higher basis via superior location, finishes, and amenities, or face legacy-asset competition in the $1.4k–$2.3k rent band.

stories.title: Whole Foods to Open Daily Shop at Murray Hill’s 509 Third Avenue
stories.excerpt: Whole Foods Market has leased a 9,000-square-foot retail space in Manhattan’s Murray Hill neighborhood. The 15-year deal occupies a ground-floor space and outdoor terraces at 509 Third Avenue, according to a memorandum of lease filed in city records Friday morning. The 35-story, 229-unit apartment tower, known as the Murray, was developed by Kahen Properties with Lalezarian Properties. A spokesperson for Whole Foods confirmed the lease in an email to Commercial Observer, but declined to share further details. Whole Foods’ newest Manhattan location will be on the smaller side. The store will follow the Amazon-owned grocer’s new Whole Foods Market Daily Shop format. The quick-trip urban shops sell grab-and-go meals alongside fresh produce, meat, bakery items and local specialty foods, according to the company’s website. The format was first rolled out in nearby Lenox Hill in 2024, and has since arrived in cities nationwide. Additional locations in Brooklyn and Hoboken, N.J., were announced late last year. Most recently, the grocer signed a lease for 8,121 square feet to open a daily shop at 1524 Second Avenue on the Upper East Side. Kahen Properties’ Majid Kahen signed the lease memorandum for the landlord, while Paul Hilliard, vice president of real estate at Whole Foods, signed for the grocer. It is unclear whether either party worked with an outside brokerage. The asking rent for the ground-floor space was not disclosed in the memorandum, but retail space in the nearby Herald Square area was $394 per square foot during the second quarter of 2026, according to CBRE data. Spokespeople for Kahen and Lalezarian Properties did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Emily Davis can be reached at edavis@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Whole Foods leased 9k SF ground floor + terrace at 509 Third Ave, Murray Hill, Manhattan; 15-year deal.
Daily Shop format (quick-trip, grab-and-go); second Manhattan location after Lenox Hill (2024).
229-unit Murray tower (Kahen/Lalezarian); grocery tenant anchors residential value in dense Manhattan neighborhood.
stories.summary: Whole Foods Market signed a 15-year ground-floor lease for 9,000 SF at 509 Third Avenue in Manhattan's Murray Hill, occupying space within the 229-unit residential tower 'the Murray.' The grocer will operate a Whole Foods Daily Shop, a smaller-format quick-trip model first rolled out in nearby Lenox Hill in 2024. Additional locations are planned for Brooklyn and Hoboken.
stories.impact: Critical signal for Manhattan multifamily: Amazon-owned Whole Foods' expansion of Daily Shop format validates dense, walkable residential neighborhoods (Murray Hill, Lenox Hill) as anchor-tenant markets. Grocery tenancy reduces resident friction (walkable food access) and supports higher rents and retention in Class A multifamily. For developers in Manhattan and urban-density markets (Boston, D.C., SF), grocer presence is material amenity—signals demand for convenience retail and supports mixed-use ground-floor pro formas. The Daily Shop rollout suggests national urban-multifamily play; developers should anticipate grocery-anchored retail at their ground floors in high-density infill.

stories.title: Medical Outpatient Building Sales Surge in H1 2026
stories.excerpt: Improving capital market conditions, expanding lender appetite and resilient operating fundamentals have driven a surge in medical outpatient building (MOB) investment sales activity, Cushman & Wakefield reported. MOB transaction volume reached $6.7 billion in the first half of 2026, a 21% increase year-over-year. MOB cap rates, meanwhile, declined 35 basis points Y-O-Y to 6.8%, while average asset pricing reached $368 per square foot in Q2 2026. Portfolio transaction activity more than doubled relative to H1 2025, exceeding $2.6 billion, as the portfolio premium widened to 100 bps over single-asset cap rates. “Cap rate compression, renewed debt market liquidity, and rising portfolio demand all point to improving investor confidence, while steady rent growth and high occupancy levels reinforce the sector’s underlying fundamentals,” said Sandy Romero, head of office & alternatives research at Cushman & Wakefield. “With capital becoming more readily available, we expect MOBs to remain well-positioned to attract institutional investment through the balance of 2026.” The post Medical Outpatient Building Sales Surge in H1 2026 appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Medical outpatient building (MOB) sales: $6.7B in H1 2026, +21% YoY; cap rates 6.8%, down 35 bps.
Portfolio premiums widened to 100 bps; avg pricing $368/SF; portfolio volume doubled to $2.6B+ versus H1 2025.
Renewed debt liquidity, resilient operating fundamentals, rent growth and high occupancy driving institutional capital.
stories.summary: Medical outpatient building investment sales surged to $6.7 billion in H1 2026, up 21% year-over-year, with cap rates compressing 35 basis points to 6.8%. Portfolio transaction volume more than doubled to $2.6 billion, and portfolio premiums widened to 100 bps over single-asset cap rates. Improving lender appetite, steady rent growth, and high occupancy sustained investor confidence across the sector.
stories.impact: Minimal direct impact on multifamily; this is a healthcare CRE story. However, capital rotation signal: as MOB cap rates compress toward multifamily levels (6.8% vs. ~5.5–6.0% for Class A multifamily in major metros), institutional mega-funds are increasingly competitive across asset types. For multifamily developers, this means equity and debt competition will remain tight—healthcare and industrial have proven cash-on-cash resilience, so multifamily basis will need to prove superior rent growth or demographic tailwinds to justify higher leverage or lower equity returns.

stories.title: Genentech Tops Out $2B Holly Springs Manufacturing Facility
stories.excerpt: Genentech raised the final beam of its new manufacturing facility in Holly Springs, North Carolina, during a topping-out ceremony. The milestone reflects continued progress on Genentech’s approximately $2 billion investment in its first-ever East Coast manufacturing facility. The project, announced in May of 2025, broke ground in August of 2025. Completion is expected in 2029. Once operational, the 700,000-square-foot facility will produce next-generation treatments for metabolic conditions, such as obesity. It will incorporate advanced biomanufacturing, automation, robotics and the latest digital manufacturing technologies designed to increase production efficiency, support sustainability, and strengthen Genentech’s U.S.-based supply chain. The project is expected to support more than 2,000 jobs, including more than 500 high-wage manufacturing roles and more than 1,500 construction jobs. The facility is part of Roche and Genentech’s broader $50 billion commitment to R&D and manufacturing infrastructure in the U.S. Roche and Genentech’s current U.S. footprint includes 13 manufacturing sites, 15 research and development sites and approximately 25,000 employees across 24 locations in eight states. The post Genentech Tops Out $2B Holly Springs Manufacturing Facility appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Genentech topped out $2B manufacturing facility in Holly Springs, North Carolina; 700k SF; completion 2029.
Project supports 2k+ jobs: 500+ high-wage manufacturing roles, 1.5k construction jobs; part of $50B Roche/Genentech U.S. commitment.
Biopharmaceutical/advanced manufacturing anchors regional employment and signals supply-chain reshoring to Southeast.
stories.summary: Genentech held a topping-out ceremony for its $2 billion, 700,000-square-foot manufacturing facility in Holly Springs, North Carolina, the company's first East Coast plant. Project began August 2025 with completion targeted 2029, supporting 2,000+ jobs including 500+ high-wage manufacturing roles. The facility will produce next-generation obesity treatments using advanced biomanufacturing, automation, and digital technologies, and is part of Roche and Genentech's broader $50 billion U.S. R&D and manufacturing infrastructure commitment.
stories.impact: Significant indirect multifamily demand driver for Holly Springs, NC, and greater Raleigh-Research Triangle region. Genentech's $2B facility and 2,000+ permanent jobs (with construction employment through 2029) will draw technical, engineering, and administrative talent to an already-growth market. This signals an opportunity for multifamily developers to acquire or entitle land in Research Triangle (Raleigh, Durham, Chapel Hill) residential submarkets now, before employer-driven migration inflates land values and construction costs. The $50B Roche/Genentech commitment flags sustained biotech/pharma clustering in the Southeast; developers should prioritize Chapel Hill and RTP-adjacent multifamily plays targeting 25–45-year-old STEM professionals with high-income-per-unit economics.

stories.title: Shifting Fortunes for L.A.’s Ports Boost Surrounding Industrial Real Estate
stories.excerpt: Ports are meant to offer protection from storms or rough seas. But nothing has been able to protect the ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach from the uncertainty and fluctuation of trade policy during President Donald Trump’s second term. “It’s like the quote from ‘The Morning Show,’” said Gregg Healy, executive vice president and head of Savills Industrial Services. “Chaos is the new cocaine. I do think we will have more turbulent times ahead.” So it’s been a welcome surprise that the tariff turbulence has seemed to benefit industrial real estate near or tied to the waterfront. From Liberation Day in April 2025, when Trump announced his first round of sweeping tariffs, to the current war with Iran, the ebbs and flows of global trade have been massive and disruptive, but new shipping volume is helping port-adjacent and port-dependent submarkets. Amid a boom and bust cycle that’s dominated the last few years, and pushing warehouse vacancy to a recent peak of 7 percent this year, Los Angeles’ industrial side may be poised for an upswing. People watch as a container ship departs from the Port of Los Angeles. PHOTO: Mario Tama/Getty Images Shipping volume at the ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach is up 1.8 percent this year. After topping 1 million container units in June, the Port of Los Angeles nearly hit that mark in July, making it the second-busiest July on record. “Businesses continue to move cargo when they see windows of opportunity amid an evolving trade environment, while resilient consumer demand is helping keep imports at historically strong levels,” said Port of Los Angeles Executive Director Gene Seroka in a recent statement. The region’s industrial market saw its highest leasing levels in five years during the second quarter of 2026, according to Cushman & Wakefield data, driven by its centrality to larger logistics networks. bullets: Port of LA/Long Beach: tariff volatility and trade disruption benefit adjacent industrial real estate despite warehouse vacancy at 7%.
Shipping volume fluctuations (Liberation Day tariffs, Iran tensions, Trump trade war) creating boom-bust cycle but new port volume.
Port-adjacent and port-dependent submarkets poised for upswing; industrial fundamentals volatile but supply-constrained.
stories.summary: Despite Trump administration tariff turbulence beginning April 2025 (Liberation Day) and ongoing geopolitical disruption (Iran tensions), Los Angeles and Long Beach ports are seeing renewed shipping volume that is unexpectedly benefiting port-adjacent industrial real estate. While general LA warehouse vacancy peaked at 7% amid boom-bust cycles over the past few years, port-dependent and waterfront-tied submarkets are experiencing incremental strength as trade flows fluctuate with policy.
stories.impact: Mixed signal for LA multifamily developers. The tariff/trade volatility creates uncertainty for industrial tenants and supply-chain logistics jobs, which are key demand drivers in LA's inland Empire and port-adjacent submarkets. However, renewed port activity and the structural advantage of Southern California's entrepôt position suggest sustained middle-wage logistics and warehouse employment—which historically supports multifamily demand in Inland Empire, Long Beach, and Vernon corridors. Developers should remain cautious on industrial-job-dependent markets (Victorville, San Bernardino) given tariff swings, but port-adjacent multifamily near LA/Long Beach may see steady demand as supply-chain nearshoring and tariff-driven re-routing of goods reinforce dwell time at West Coast ports. Monitor policy shifts quarterly; tariff reversals or trade deals could rapidly shift this calculus.

stories.title: West Palm Beach Developer Buys Lot, Apartments on Way
stories.excerpt: Estate Cos. bought a lot in West Palm Beach and plans to build the second phase of a two-phase apartment project. The S. Floirda Business Journal reports the company paid $13 million for a 1.19-acre lot at 411 West Railroad. The seller was Sunview Cos. Banesco USA provided an $8.45 million mortgage to the buyer. For the first phase, the 321-unit, eight-story Soleste Palm Station, just west of this site, is still under construction. For Phase II, The Estate Cos. plans to develop the new site with 310 apartments in 15 stories. For Soleste Palm Station Two, the multifamily community will include 411 parking spaces and a pool deck. Estate Companies says it identifies and coordinates investment opportunities for both private and institutional investors. It’s focus, since 2012, is on high-yielding, risk-adjusted, development and investment opportunities (land and residential projects) in the South Florida region. The post West Palm Beach Developer Buys Lot, Apartments on Way appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Estate Cos. acquired 1.19-acre lot, West Palm Beach for $13M; plans Phase II: 310 units, 15 stories.
Phase I: 321-unit Soleste Palm Station (8 stories) under construction nearby; Phase II adds parking, pool deck.
Banesco USA financed Phase II with $8.45M mortgage; two-phase development signals strong South Florida apartment demand.
stories.summary: Estate Companies purchased a 1.19-acre infill lot at 411 West Railroad in West Palm Beach for $13 million and plans to develop Phase II of a two-phase multifamily project. Phase I, the 321-unit Soleste Palm Station, is currently under construction nearby. Phase II will deliver 310 apartments over 15 stories with 411 parking spaces and a pool deck. Banesco USA provided an $8.45 million construction mortgage.
stories.impact: Confirms South Florida multifamily demand resilience and developer confidence in West Palm Beach. Estate Companies' two-phase strategy—Phase I near completion, Phase II entitlement and financing in place—signals strong absorption and rent growth sufficient to justify 631-unit combined supply in a single submarket. For multifamily developers, West Palm Beach (beyond Miami/FLL core) represents emerging infill opportunity as Miami-proper faces supply saturation and rent moderation. The rapid Phase II finance (Banesco mortgage) suggests strong lender confidence in WPB market fundamentals. Developers should prioritize in-fill sites and adaptive reuse opportunities in West Palm's emerging downtown/transit corridors to capture migration from Miami before that market cools further.

stories.title: Retail Landlords Need to Underwrite Their Tenants’ Customer Base, Too
stories.excerpt: Landlords underwrite the retail tenant. But they almost never underwrite the tenant’s customer. They should. That gap costs landlords money, and it is fixable before a listing goes live. The standard leasing process is too reactive: Review comparable rents, post the space on Crexi and LoopNet, wait for responses, and then vet an operator’s finances. Mark Kvetkovskiy. None of that tells you whether enough of that retailer’s customers live near the space. If they do not, the risk rises of tenant failure, months of vacancy, and another round of commissions and negotiations. The better approach is to flip the process. Instead of waiting to see who shows up, start by studying who lives near the space. How do nearby households spend? Which categories over-index locally? Does the neighborhood support an everyday concept, a destination brand, or something in between? Answer those questions first, and you can define the customer already walking the neighborhood’s streets. Then, identify the brands that serve that customer and approach them directly about the vacancy. Proactive outreach can reduce days on market and the vacancy costs that come with them. Consider a hypothetical vacant restaurant at Rivington and Ludlow streets on Manhattan’s Lower East Side. I analyzed the 2026 Esri Consumer Spending Survey and Esri Market Potential data for the area within a five-minute walk. Esri’s modeled data draws on consumer surveys, demographic segmentation and household spending patterns. It is directional, not a record of observed transactions. Esri estimates that households in that walking area spend $50,243,250 annually on food and beverages away from home, or about $5,043 per household. The market-potential data then sharpens the picture. Some 20.4 percent of adults in the area visited a fine-dining restaurant in the previous six months, an index of 124, or 24 percent above the U.S. average. bullets: Opinion piece: retail landlords underwrite tenant finances but rarely underwrite tenant customer base; misses demand risk.
Gap analysis: if retailer's customers don't live/work near space, tenant failure risk rises; reactive leasing delays discovery.
Solution: proactive demand analysis—study neighborhood demographics, spending patterns, category over-indexing—before marketing vacancy.
stories.summary: A CRE industry perspective argues that retail landlords have long underwritten tenant operators' financial credentials but neglect underwriting the tenant's customer base—a blind spot that increases vacancy and failure risk. Reactive leasing (post to LoopNet, wait for offers, vet later) obscures whether neighborhood demographics support the retailer's concept. The better approach flips process: analyze who lives/works nearby, how they spend, which categories over-index, then proactively approach brands serving that neighborhood's customer profile.
stories.impact: Tangential to multifamily development but strategically important for mixed-use and ground-floor retail strategy in residential projects. Multifamily developers and joint-venture retail partners should adopt demand-first leasing: analyze residential community's demographic profile, household income, age, and consumer behavior BEFORE designing ground-floor retail or entering LOIs with anchor tenants. This directly impacts residential unit valuations—weak retail tenancy or high turnover erodes street activation, perceived safety, and NOI. For mixed-use projects in secondary markets or new neighborhoods (e.g., West Palm Beach, emerging Texas suburbs), pre-lease ground floor to a retailer whose customer profile matches your resident demographic, or accept higher tenant concessions/lower rents. Reverse: if multifamily tenant income/age misaligns with typical grocer/restaurant customer, expect higher retail vacancy and longer recapture periods.

stories.title: T&E Development Buys West Chelsea Site for $34M From PPHE Hotel Group
stories.excerpt: A development site in Manhattan’s West Chelsea area previously conceived for hotel and luxury residences in 2019 by an international hospitality firm is now poised for a new residential journey. Amsterdam-based PPHE Hotel Group sold the property at 538-542 West 29th Street to Brooklyn-based T&E Development for $33.5 million in a deal that closed late Thursday afternoon, Commercial Observer has learned. Colliers represented the seller with a team led by Zach Redding, Dylan Kane and Jared King. Sporn Group’s Lenny Sporn arranged the sale on behalf of the buyer. Crain’s New York Business first reported that the deal was set to close this summer. PPHE Hotel Group announced in March 2019 it had formed a joint venture with developer Largo to acquire the vacant lot for around $42 million, with plans to build a 98-key hotel and 55 condos. An entity connected to PPHE field demolition permits for the project in late 2023, Crain’s reported at the time. Greg Hegarty, co-CEO of PPHE, said in a February statement on the pending sale that “significant changes to the regulatory landscape” for ground-up development of hotel projects in New York following its 2019 acquisition contributed to the decision to part ways with the property. The 9,875-square-foot vacant lot between 10th and 11th avenues has 74,063 square feet of development potential under New York City’s C6-3 zoning within the Special West Chelsea District and will not require an affordable housing component, according to Colliers. T&E recently completed a 54-unit condo development called the Florian at 350 East 18th Street in Manhattan’s Gramercy Park. Redding said the property is one of the few remaining unconstrained development sites in West Chelsea and would be well positioned as a residential project given there is only one condo building currently under construction between West 20th and West 30th streets. bullets: T&E Development acquired West Chelsea site (538-542 West 29th St, Manhattan) from PPHE Hotel Group for $33.5M.
Property was planned as 98-key hotel + 55 condos by PPHE/Largo JV (acquired 2019 for ~$42M); site vacant.
Shift from hotel to residential reflects Manhattan market dynamic; soft hotel demand, strong residential pricing.
stories.summary: Brooklyn-based T&E Development purchased the West Chelsea site at 538-542 West 29th Street from Amsterdam-based PPHE Hotel Group for $33.5 million in a deal that closed late last week. PPHE and developer Largo had acquired the vacant lot in March 2019 for approximately $42 million with plans to build a 98-room hotel and 55 condos. PPHE filed demolition permits in late 2023 but pivoted to sale, signaling strategy shift away from hotel in favor of capital redeployment.
stories.impact: Critical market signal: Hotel-to-residential conversion (or purpose-shift) in Manhattan prime real estate (West Chelsea, Chelsea Market proximity) reflects persistent soft hotel demand post-pandemic and superior residential valuations in core Manhattan. PPHE's $42M acquisition (2019) to $33.5M sale (2026) signals capital loss on hotel-condo project, but T&E's residential-only rebrand validates residential-as-safer asset class in Manhattan. For developers: prime Manhattan sites are reverting from mixed-use hotel/condo to pure residential or rental. This signals opportunity for developers with pure-residential expertise and capital discipline to acquire entitlement-stage Manhattan sites from hospitality operators at distressed prices. Conversely, hotel-condo hybrid deals in NYC face financing and absorption headwinds—pure rental or pure-for-sale residential commands cleaner underwriting and lender support. Expect more hotel->residential asset transitions in secondary Manhattan CBDs (Chelsea, Hells Kitchen, LES) as hotel demand remains weak relative to pre-pandemic.
